                                                  ON A WEISS-TYPE ALMOST MONOTONICITY
                                                                FORMULA

                                                                             AELSON SOBRAL




arXiv:2604.12712v2 [math.AP] 27 Apr 2026
                                                  Abstract. We establish a Weiss-type almost-monotonicity formula for
                                                  a broad class of variable-coefficient energy functionals, assuming only
                                                  minimal regularity of the coefficients. As an application, we classify
                                                  blow-up limits for the Alt–Phillips problem with variable coefficients
                                                  under significantly weaker regularity hypotheses than those imposed in
                                                  Araújo et al. [Calc. Var. Partial Differential Equations, 65, no. 1, Paper
                                                  No. 24 (2026)]. Moreover, by means of a distinct argument, we extend
                                                  the corresponding free-boundary regularity result. We conclude with a
                                                  discussion of further extensions, including two-phase analogues.




                                                                           1. Introduction
                                              For a bounded domain Ω ⊂ Rd and a measurable, locally bounded func-
                                           tion σ : Ω × R+ → R+ , we consider almost minimizers to the functional
                                                                     Z                          
                                                                         1
                                                         J (u, Ω) :=       ⟨A(x)∇u, ∇u⟩ + σ(x, u) dx,           (1.1)
                                                                      Ω 2
                                           where A(x) is a uniformly elliptic matrix-valued function. In this work, we
                                           establish a new Weiss-type almost monotonicity formula, which proves to
                                           be an effective tool for classifying homogeneity in a broad class of problems.
                                           Several applications illustrating the scope of this result are also discussed.
                                              Monotonicity formulae of Weiss-type, when available, are key to analyzing
                                           the fine structure of the free-boundary. One of the major developments is
                                           the homogeneity approach introduced by Weiss [15], which constitutes the
                                           main object of study in this paper. Further extensions and generalizations
                                           include the Alt–Caffarelli–Friedman monotonicity formula [3], the Monneau-
                                           type monotonicity formula [13], and the Caffarelli–Jerison–Kenig result [7].
                                              The goal of this paper is to establish a Weiss-type monotonicity formula
                                           for a broad class of energy functionals of the form (1.1). We will specify the
                                           precise assumptions on the ingredients later, but the key point is that both
                                           terms in the energy involve variable coefficients, which may complicate the
                                           analysis of the associated free boundary. Since these coefficients possess only
                                               Date: April 28, 2026.
                                               2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. Primary 35R35. Secondary 35A21.
                                               Key words and phrases. Monotonicity formula, Free boundary problems, Non-
                                           differentiable functionals.
                                                                                      1
2                                 A. SOBRAL

limited regularity, minimizers are not expected to satisfy the standard Weiss
monotonicity formula. Instead, we derive an almost (or quasi) monotonicity
formula, in which an error term quantifies the deviation from monotonicity
depending on how far the coefficients are from being constant. Under mini-
mal regularity assumptions, this formulation still allows for the classification
of homogeneous blow-ups.
   The main idea is conceptually simple and relies on the optimal regularity
of the solution near free boundary points. The strategy consists in freezing
the coefficients: for x0 ∈ F (u), we consider
                           Z                               
                                1
             Jx0 (u, Ω) :=        ⟨A(x0 )∇u, ∇u⟩ + σ(x0 , u) dx,
                            Ω 2
and use optimal regularity to compare this with the original functional,
by testing against a suitable competitor and then comparing back to the
“frozen-at-x0 ” energy functional. This back-and-forth comparison requires
some regularity of the coefficients; however, once optimal regularity for mini-
mizers is established, the assumptions on the coefficients can be significantly
weakened. This is precisely why the resulting formula is of almost mono-
tonicity type. We focus primarily on one-phase Alt–Phillips-type problems,
though the same approach can be extended to other kinds of variable coef-
ficient functionals with possibly two-phases, see Section 5.
   The terminology almost monotonicity (or quasi monotonicity) appears in
the literature in various contexts, though typically for problems of a different
nature. We refer to [10] and [13], where almost monotonicity formulas were
established for both elliptic and parabolic equations, extending the results of
[7] and the earlier works of Caffarelli and Kenig. In the context of Weiss- and
Monneau-type formulas, we mention [11], which treats the obstacle problem
with Lipschitz coefficients and employs these ideas to extend the classical
analyses of Caffarelli, Monneau, and Weiss. To the best of our knowledge,
this is the first work where such an approach is developed for Alt–Phillips-
type problems under very low regularity assumptions on the coefficients.
   Even though our class of energy functionals is fairly general, and we work
with almost minimizers, our main focus lies on the specific case
                               |∇u|2
                         Z                      
                                     + δ(x) uγ(x) dx,
                           Ω     2
where δ is bounded away from zero and γ(x) ∈ [min γ, max γ] ⋐ (0, 1). This
problem was previously studied in [5], while the version with variable coef-
ficients was investigated in [6]. In those works, the full regularity program
was carried out, from the analysis of the solutions up to the regularity of
the free boundary. In the present paper, we address the final step of that
program, substantially relaxing the regularity assumptions on both δ and γ
             ON A WEISS-TYPE ALMOST MONOTONICITY FORMULA                           3

to a more natural setting:
                       δ ∈ C 0,Dini   and   γ ∈ C 0,log -Dini .
In contrast, [5] required δ, γ ∈ W 1,q for some q > d, a considerably stronger
assumption. Determining whether our monotonicity formula applies in full
generality lies beyond the scope of this paper and is left for future inves-
tigation. In particular, we establish the homogeneity of blow-ups for the
problem considered in [6], as well as for the Alt–Caffarelli functional with
variable coefficients and its two-phase versions.
   The approach developed in this paper suggests several natural directions
for future work. A first question is whether the strategy of [1] can be adapted
to the present setting and, if so, what regularity assumptions it would im-
pose on the coefficients. This is not immediate, since in our problem the
right-hand side also contains variable coefficients. Another direction is to
identify the weakest coefficient regularity under which free-boundary regu-
larity persists, both for the problem studied in [6] and for the Alt–Caffarelli
problem discussed in Section 5. A further challenging problem is to de-
velop a monotonicity-based framework yielding a p-Laplacian analogue of
the monotonicity formula adapted to the problem studied in [14].
   The paper is organized as follows. We give the formula and proof in
Section 3. In Section 4, we give two applications of this new almost mono-
tonicity formula. Finally, in Section 5, we show how the formula can be
extended to other scenarios.



                    2. Definitions and preliminaries
  This section is devoted to establishing the mathematical setting of the
paper. We fix notation and collect preliminary definitions and known results
that will be used in the sequel.


2.1. Mathematical setup and assumptions. Given a domain Ω ⊂ Rd ,
we say that u ≥ 0 is an almost minimizer to
                      Z                              
                           1
             J (w) :=        ⟨A(x)∇w, ∇w⟩ + δ(x) wγ(x) dx, (2.1)
                           2
in Ω, if for every r > 0 and x0 ∈ Rd such that Br (x0 ) ⊂ Ω, we have
     J (u, Br (x0 )) ≤ (1 + ϱ(r)) J (v, Br (x0 ))      ∀ v ∈ u + H01 (Br (x0 )).
where                     Z                                      
                           1
          J (w, O) :=        ⟨A(x)∇w, ∇w⟩ + δ(x) wγ(x)                dx.
                       O   2
When ϱ ≡ 0, we say that u is a local minimizer.
4                                     A. SOBRAL

  Central to the analysis in this paper is the notion of the Alt–Phillips
functional frozen at x0 . For a given x0 ∈ Rn , we set
                         Z                                    
                              1
         Jx0 (w, O) :=          ⟨A(x0 )∇w, ∇w⟩ + δ(x0 ) wγ(x0 ) dx.
                          O 2


   The basic assumptions on A, δ, γ, and ϱ are the following. The mapping
A : Ω 7→ Ssym (d) is continuous, where Ssym (d) denotes the space of symmetric
d×d matrices. We assume that A is uniformly elliptic: there exists Λ ∈ (0, 1]
such that
          ⟨A(x)ξ, ξ⟩ ∈ Λ, Λ−1 for every x ∈ Ω and |ξ| = 1.
                               

Moreover,
                                                          
                inf δ, sup δ ⋐ (0, ∞),           inf γ, sup γ ⋐ (0, 1),
                Ω      Ω                         Ω      Ω
so that δ is bounded away from 0, and γ stays a positive distance away from
both 0 and 1. Finally, we assume that the gauge function ϱ is a modulus of
continuity.
   We denote by ωA , ωδ , and ωγ the moduli of continuity of A, δ, and γ,
respectively. The precise continuity assumptions imposed on A, δ, γ, and
ϱ will be specified in the statements of the main results. Throughout the
paper, the notation ≲ means inequality up to a multiplicative universal
constant; here and in what follows, universal indicates dependence only on
the dimension d, the ellipticity constant Λ, and the bounds for δ and γ.
   We also assume a quantitative growth control for u near free boundary
points. More precisely, for every x0 ∈ ∂{u > 0} ∩ Ω and every ball Br (x0 ) ⊂
Ω, we require                                2   
                     sup     u(x) + |∇u(x)| γ(x0 ) ≲ rβ(x0 ) ,          (2.2)
                    x∈Br (x0 )
where
                                            2
                                 β(x0 ) :=         .
                                        2 − γ(x0 )
Such growth estimates are available in several relevant settings; we refer the
reader to [5, 6] for further discussion.


2.2. Free boundary and pointwise homogeneity. Throughout the pa-
per, we focus on one-phase almost minimizers u to the functional (2.1) in
Ω = B2 . The Weiss-type almost monotonicity formula proved in the next
section should also extend to the two-phase setting, provided the correspond-
ing growth assumptions are available, as discussed in the introduction.
   The growth assumption (2.2) is crucial for the fine analysis of the free
boundary
                           F (u) := ∂{u > 0} ∩ B2 .
            ON A WEISS-TYPE ALMOST MONOTONICITY FORMULA                             5

In particular, it allows us to introduce blow-up sequences at free boundary
points x0 ∈ F (u) by setting
                 ur (x) := r−β(x0 ) u(x0 + rx),        r ∈ (0, 1).
By the scaling properties of the functional, together with nondegeneracy
and the compactness of (almost) minimizers, for every sequence rk ↓ 0 there
exists a subsequence (still denoted rk ) such that urk → u0 locally in Rn , for
some nontrivial limit u0 ̸≡ 0.
  The Weiss-type almost monotonicity formula proved in the next section
implies that every blow-up limit u0 is homogeneous about 0, with homo-
geneity exponent β(x0 ). More precisely,
                   u0 (λx) = λβ(x0 ) u0 (x)       for all λ ≥ 0.
After the blow-up procedure, we may distinguish the free boundary points
into two kinds. We say that x0 is a regular point of F (u) if at least one
blow-up limit is of the form
                                         β(x )
                   u0 (x) = ϑ(x0 ) (x · ν)+ 0 ,       ν ∈ ∂B1 ,
and we refer to such profiles as trivial cones. The constant ϑ(x0 ) is chosen
so that u0 solves the Alt–Phillips equation with coefficients frozen at x0 ,
namely
                                      γ(x )−1
                 ∆u0 = δ(x0 )γ(x0 ) u0 0       in {u0 > 0}.
The precise expression for ϑ(x0 ) is given in Section 4.
   We denote the set of regular points by R(u) and define the singular set
by
                            Σ(u) := F (u) \ R(u),
so that
                            F (u) = R(u) ∪ Σ(u).
Finally, when a β(x0 )-homogeneous blow-up is not a trivial cone, we call it
a nontrivial minimal cone. We emphasize that this notion depends on the
base point x0 at which the blow-up is taken.


2.3. Known results. We state a Lemma that gives compactness of mini-
mizers, as well as convergence of free boundaries. Its proof is rather stan-
dard, but we bring it here for completeness.

Since Br (x0 ) ⊂ Ω and v ∈ u + H 1 (Br (x0 )) were arbitrary, this shows that u
is an almost minimizer (with the same gauge ϱ) of J in Ω.
   Next, we show that
                      χ{uk >0} → χ{u>0}            in L1loc (Ω).
Since 0 ≤ χ{uk >0} ≤ 1, the dominated convergence theorem reduces the
claim to proving
                 χ{uk >0} (x) → χ{u>0} (x)          for a.e. x ∈ Ω.
By the uniform nondegeneracy of uk (and hence of the limit u), the free
boundary ∂{u > 0} has Lebesgue measure zero, so we may restrict the
analysis to
                                 x ∈ Ω \ ∂{u > 0}.
If u(x) > 0, then, by continuity, there exists rx > 0 such that Brx (x) ⊂ {u >
0} ∩ Ω. Uniform convergence uk → u implies that uk > 0 in Brx /2 (x) for all
sufficiently large k, hence χ{uk >0} (x) = 1 = χ{u>0} (x).
   If instead x ∈ {u = 0}◦ , there exists rx > 0 such that Brx (x) ⊂ {u =
0} ∩ Ω. We claim that Brx /2 (x) ⊂ {uk = 0} for all large k. Otherwise,
along a subsequence, there would exist yk ∈ Brx /2 (x) with uk (yk ) > 0, and
so Brx /2 (x) intersects F (uk ). If we take
                         xk ∈ Brx /2 (x) ∩ ∂{uk > 0},
Then, by uniform nondegeneracy at the free boundary point xk , we have
                       sup uk ≥      sup         uk ≥ c ς(rx ).
                      Brx (x)     Brx /2 (xk )

However, since u ≡ 0 in Brx (x) and uk → u uniformly, we have supBrx (x) uk →
0, a contradiction. Hence Brx /2 (x) ⊂ {uk = 0} for all large k, and therefore
χ{uk >0} (x) = 0 = χ{u>0} (x). In conclusion, χ{uk >0} (x) → χ{u>0} (x) for a.e.
x ∈ Ω.
   Finally, we prove the convergence of the free boundaries. Let K ⋐ Ω.
From the previous argument, if Br (x) ⊂ {u > 0} (respectively Br (x) ⊂ {u =
0}), then for k large enough Br/2 (x) ⊂ {uk > 0} (respectively Br/2 (x) ⊂
{uk = 0}). Hence, for every ε > 0 and all large k,
               F (uk ) ∩ K ⊂ {y ∈ K : dist(y, ∂{u > 0}) < ε}.
8                                      A. SOBRAL

Conversely, if x ∈ F (u) ∩ K and along a subsequence dist(x, F (uk )) ≥ ε,
then either Bε (x) ⊂ {uk > 0} or Bε (x) ⊂ {uk = 0} along that subsequence.
By uniform convergence this would force Bε/2 (x) ⊂ {u > 0} or Bε/2 (x) ⊂
{u = 0}, contradicting x ∈ F (u). Thus, for each x ∈ F (u) ∩ K there exist
xk ∈ F (uk ) with xk → x. These two inclusions imply the local Hausdorff
convergence of F (uk ) to F (u).                                        □


                        3. Weiss almost monotonicity
   In this section, we state and prove the main result of the paper: a Weiss-
type almost monotonicity formula that applies to almost minimizers to (2.1).
As an immediate consequence, we obtain the homogeneity of blow-up limits.
The approach developed here significantly reduces the regularity assump-
tions required on the coefficients δ and γ compared to [5]. We focus here on
the one-phase case and explain in Section 5 how the argument extends to
the two-phase setting.

B2 . Assume further that
    ωA (·) + ωδ (·) + ϱ(·) + | ln(·)|ωγ (·) ∈ C 0,dini ([0, 2])   and   A(x0 ) = Id ,

Remark 3.1. The assumption g ∈ L1 is needed to guarantee that the limit

  As a corollary of the Weiss-type almost monotonicity formula, every blow-

Remark 3.2.

        4. The Alt–Philips problem with varying coefficients
   In this section, we revisit fine regularity properties of the free boundary
of nonnegative local minimizers of the so-called ‘Alt–Philips problem with
             ON A WEISS-TYPE ALMOST MONOTONICITY FORMULA                     13

varying coefficients’
                                       |∇u|2
                                 Z                           
                    Jδγ (u) :=               + δ(x) uγ(x)         dx.     (4.1)
                                         2
Local minimizers to this functional were studied in detail in the recent work
[5], in which the main result is that if
                                      1,q
                             δ, γ ∈ Wloc     for     q > d,
then the free boundary F (u) ∩ B1 is locally a C 1,γ surface up to a negligible
set Σ(u) of Hausdorff dimension less than or equal to d − 3. Moreover, if
                                             2,∞
                                    δ, γ ∈ Wloc  ,
then Hd−1 (F (u) ∩ Br ) ≲ rd−1 .
   At first glance, both assumptions may appear to impose an excessively
high degree of regularity; however, they arise naturally from classical meth-
ods. The standard derivation of the Weiss monotonicity formula requires
differentiating the functional once, while the derivation of Hausdorff measure
estimates for the Alt–Phillips problem requires differentiating the equation
twice. In this framework, both assumptions are essentially sharp, as they
are needed to control the error terms generated by the derivatives of γ and
δ. The reasoning here in this section allows us to significantly reduce these
regularity assumptions to
                             dini                       log −dini
                        δ ∈ Cloc       and         γ ∈ Cloc       .       (4.2)
   The main building blocks to that end are that
     (I) R(u) is locally open in F (u);
    (II) Flatness implies regularity;
   (III) Dimension reduction argument,
which we prove in the forthcoming subsections. Item (I) is essentially a
consequence of the Weiss monotonicity formula. Item (II) was established,
in essence, in [5, Section 7]. In that work, we assumed that both δ and
γ were Hölder continuous, as a consequence of the W 1,q assumption with
q > d. However, the argument only requires that, after scaling, both δ and γ
become almost constant. We also emphasize that, within the positivity set,
the solution is classical in view of the continuity assumptions on δ and γ,
together with Kovats’ borderline regularity results [12]. Item (III) likewise
follows from the Weiss monotonicity formula and the translation invariance
of homogeneous blow-ups. We summarize these conclusions in the following
theorem.
Theorem 4.1. Let u ≥ 0 be a local minimizer to the energy-functional
(4.1) in B2 . Assume further that Assumption (4.2) is in force. Then, R(u)
is locally C 1,α , and
                           dimH (Σ(u)) ≤ d − 3.
14                                 A. SOBRAL

Moreover, Hd−1 (F (u) ∩ Br ) ≲ rd−1 , for r ≤ 1.

  We divide the proof of this theorem into several parts to make the argu-
ment more easily followable.

4.1. The regular set is locally open. Let x0 ∈ R(u). By definition, the
family (ur )r>0 , defined by
                          ur (x) := r−β(x0 ) u(x0 + rx)
                                                                         β(x )
converges, up to subsequence, to the trivial cone ux0 (x) := ϑ(x0 )(x · ν)+ 0 ,
for some vector ν ∈ ∂B1 . The constant ϑ(x0 ) is chosen so that ux0 is a local
minimizer to the Alt–Philips functional frozen at x0
                           |∇u|2
                      Z                          
                                           γ(x0 )
                                 + δ(x0 ) u         dx.
                             2
The precise value of the constant ϑ(x0 ) is
                                                 1
                               (β(x0 ) − 1)β(x0 ) γ(x0 )−2
                   ϑ(x0 ) :=                               .
                                  γ(x0 ) δ(x0 )
The Weiss energy of those functions is constant and depends on the values
of γ and δ applied to x0 . This is a direct computation based on its explicit
form.
                                                    β(x )
Lemma 4.1. Let x0 ∈ Rd , ux0 (x) := ϑ(x0 )(x · ν)+ 0 with ν ∈ ∂B1 , and
Au,0 (·) be the Weiss energy defined in Theorem 3.1. Then, there is V de-
pending on the values of γ, δ applied on x0 , and dimension such that
                     Aux0 ,0 (r) = V(x0 )   for all   r > 0.
Moreover, V, as a function of x0 , is continuous and its modulus of continuity
depends on those of γ and δ.

  Now we prove an energy gap for the Weiss energy. The proof is essentially
the same as that for the constant parameter, but we include it here for
completeness.

Proposition 4.1. Let u ≥ 0 be a local minimizer to the energy-functional
(4.1) in B2 , U be a blow up at a point z0 ∈ F (u) that is a nontrivial minimal
cone, and AU,0 its Weiss energy. Assume further that Assumption (4.2) is
in force. Then, there exists a universal constant η > 0 such that
                              AU,0 ≥ V(z0 ) + η.                          (4.3)

Proof. For simplicity, we assume z0 = 0 and write AU ≡ AU,0 . First, we
prove the strict inequality AU > V(0). Assume, toward a contradiction,
that
                               AU ≤ V(0).
            ON A WEISS-TYPE ALMOST MONOTONICITY FORMULA                               15

Let X0 ∈ R(U ) be a regular free boundary point, and consider the blow-up
sequence
                       Ur (X) := r−β(0) U (X0 + rX).
Taking a subsequence if necessary, it converges to a half-space solution of
the form
                                    β(0)
               U0 (X) = ϑ(0) (X · ν)+     for some ν ∈ ∂B1 .
In particular, by Lemma 2.1, U0 is a local minimizer of the functional
                             |∇v|2
                        Z                      
                                           γ(0)
                                   + δ(0)v        dx,                  (4.4)
                               2
and the Weiss energy of U0 around 0 equals V(0). Since U is β(0)-homogeneous

                 Ur (X) = U X + r−1 X0      for all X ∈ Rd ,
                                        

and therefore
       AU,X0 (r) = AUr ,r−1 X0 (1)
                                                        Z
                                    −1          1
                 = J0 (Ur , B1 (r        X0 )) − β(0)                   Ur2 dHd−1 .
                                                2       ∂B1 (r−1 X0 )
By the convergence of Ur to U0 and the contradiction assumption, we obtain
                       lim AU,X0 (r) = AU,0 (1) ≤ V(0).
                       r→∞
On the other hand, since X0 is a regular point, we have
                             lim AU,X0 (r) = V(0).
                             r→0
Since r 7→ AU,X0 (r) is monotone nondecreasing, it must be constant and
equal to V(0) for all r > 0. This implies that U is β(0)-homogeneous with
respect to X0 . Hence U is a cone with vertex at X0 as well as at 0, and
therefore must be a half-space solution, contradicting the assumption that
U is nontrivial. This can be proved by induction in dimension, as in [16,
Proof of Proposition 8.1]. This proves AU > V(0).
   We now show that the strict inequality is quantitative, i.e. (4.3) holds for
some universal η > 0. Assume not. Then there exist nontrivial minimizing
cones Uk for functional (4.4) and numbers ηk ↓ 0 such that
                               AUk < V(0) + ηk .
By the preceding argument, we also have AUk ≥ V(0), hence
                          AUk → V(0)          as   k → ∞.
Using compactness of minimizers, we may assume
                     Uk → U∞         locally uniformly in Rd ,
16                                      A. SOBRAL

where U∞ is a minimizing cone. By the lower semicontinuity of the Weiss
energy and the limit above,
                                      AU∞ = V(0),
and so, in view of the preceding argument, U∞ must be the trivial cone.
Since Uk → U∞ , for k sufficiently large the free boundaries F (Uk ) are suf-
ficiently flat in B1 . By the “flatness implies regularity” theorem for the
constant-parameter Alt–Phillips functional, each F (Uk ) is C 1 in B1 for k
large. Because Uk is homogeneous with respect to 0, the set F (Uk ) is a
cone:
                   x ∈ F (Uk ) =⇒ λx ∈ F (Uk )        ∀λ > 0.
In particular, F (Uk ) is a C 1 conical hypersurface with vertex at 0, and hence
it must be a hyperplane. Therefore {Uk > 0} is a half-space.
   Finally, in a half-space the only nonnegative β(0)-homogeneous minimizer
of the frozen Alt–Phillips functional is the half-space solution
                                                        β(0)
                              Uk (X) = ϑ(0) (X · ν)+ .
This contradicts the choice of Uk as nontrivial minimizing cones.                    □

   As a consequence of the energy gap, we obtain that R(u) is locally open
in F (u).

Theorem 4.2. Let u ≥ 0 be a local minimizer to the energy-functional (4.1)
in B2 . Assume further that Assumption (4.2) is in force. It follows that
                                  dimH (Σ(u)) ≤ d − 3.

from which the conclusion of the Theorem follows.                                  □

4.3. Hausdorff measure estimates. In this subsection, we prove that the

   A proper iteration of Lemma 4.2 gives the Hausdorff measure estimate
for the free boundary.

Indeed, let x ∈ F (u) ∩ B1 . If there is k ∈ N such that x ∈ Gk , then so it is
in G∞ . If there is no k ∈ N such that x ∈ Gk , then it means that x ∈ Ek
for every k ∈ N, which implies that x ∈ E∞ . This proves the inclusion
(4.17). Finally, we argue that Hd−1 (G∞ ) ≲ 1, and Hd−1 (E∞ ) = 0. While
Hd−1 (G∞ ) ≲ 1 follows from the fact that Gk is a increasing sequence of sets
with, by (4.13), Hd−1 (Gk ) ≲ 1, to show that Hd−1 (E∞ ) = 0 we recall that

                               5. Further extensions
   In this section, we bring some extensions of the almost monotonicity for-
mula that include the one-phase Alt-Caffarelli problem which was introduced
in [2], its two-phase version, and the Alt–Philips problem with varying co-
efficients.


5.1. The Alt–Caffarelli one-phase problem. Let Q and A be contin-
uous functions, bounded from below away from zero. The Alt–Caffarelli
functional is defined as
                       Z                             
                           1
              J (u) :=       ⟨A(x)∇u, ∇u⟩ + Q(x)X{u>0} dx.     (5.1)
                           2
     Here is the almost monotonicity formula.

Corollary 5.1. Let u ≥ 0 be a local minimizer to the functional (5.1) in
B2 . Assume further that
                ωA (·) + ωQ (·) + ϱ(·) ∈ C 0,dini           and       A(x0 ) = Id ,
for x0 ∈ F (u) ∩ B1 . Then, blow-ups are 1-homogeneous.

Remark 5.1. We observe that we do not need the function Q to be bounded
from below. This is only necessary to ensure nondegeneracy. Also, for local
minimizer, Lipschitz regularity is available by the regularity result from [9].

5.2. The two-phase case. Both Alt–Caffarelli and Alt–Phillips mono-
tonicity formulas can be extended to the two-phase scenario, provided that
optimal regularity is still available at the free boundary points where we
do the blow-up procedure. For instance, in the Alt–Caffarelli scenarion, we
28                                          A. SOBRAL

may consider the following functional
           Z                                              
               1
  J (u) :=       ⟨A(x)∇u, ∇u⟩ + Q1 (x)X{u>0} + Q2 (x)X{u<0} dx.                                 (5.6)
               2

        ωA (·) + ωQ1 (·) + ωQ2 (·) + ϱ(·) ∈ C 0,dini                and         A(x0 ) = Id ,

is almost monotone, in the sense that there exists a nonnegative real function

                            d

                            dr

parison between the original and frozen functionals yields one additional
term.                                                                  □

Remark 5.2. We remark that the growth estimate for u at free bound-
ary points may be hard to obtain, depending on whether x0 is a two-phase
branching free boundary point or not.
